items.summary: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.
items.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

items.summary: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
items.title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

items.summary: Overview: This deposit hosts the official replication package, synthetic benchmark dataset, and experimental audit artifacts for the scientific manuscript: "M-11: Auditing Synthetic Risk Labels and Physical Baselines in a Cyber-Physical Benchmark for Underground Mining" (submitted to Acta Montanistica Slovaca , 2026). M-11 is a simulation-only cyber-physical benchmark that integrates AI4I 2020 predictive maintenance attributes with synthetic kinematic positioning, physiological, and environmental indicators (10,000 records; 37 columns) to audit the statistical mechanics and potential circularity of synthetic risk labelling in confined underground mining operations. Key Empirical Findings Reported in the Manuscript: Label Circularity Audit: Variance decomposition demonstrates that 82.07% of the synthetic score variance is driven by spatial/kinematic components, 17.43% by injected noise, 0.48% by multimodal variables, and 0.02% by cross-covariance. Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. The paired bootstrap difference (ΔF2 = -0.0038, 95% CI: -0.0129 to 0.0047) and Holm-adjusted McNemar test (p = 0.6015) confirm no statistically significant gap under circular labels. Decoupled Hazard Stress Tests: Under 22% class prevalence and low signal-to-noise ratio, non-spatial decoupled labels (CO, fatigue, vibration) push F2 optimisation to near-universal HIGH alerts, approaching the trivial Always-HIGH baseline (F2 = 0.5851). A multimodal-only composite target recovers F2 = 0.6408 with 54.1% specificity. Feature Ablations: Removing three direct kinematic indicators reduces F2 by 9.60 percentage points; removing the entire 8-feature spatial block reduces F2 by 32.52 percentage points from the full 0.9065 baseline. Computational Scalability: Local backend P95 latency scales to 27.91 ms under 500 concurrent simulated agents (< 200 ms supervisory threshold). The WebGL/Three.js integrated-GPU prototype achieves 34.8 FPS under nominal load. Deterministic Safety & GenAI Audit: The independent deterministic safety layer satisfies 17 automated unit/integration tests and 100/100 scripted regulatory scenario checks. The Gemini language model acts strictly as an exploratory natural-language interface without numerical autonomy. Package Contents & Cryptographic Verification (SHA-256): public_mining_equipment_dataset.csv (3,859,401 bytes) — SHA-256: b71d0b6baed8b6e0bc7eee1a1a5b7440d06a04ddaea5d502907cf03d958705f0 requirements.txt (574 bytes) — Frozen Python 3.10.11 scientific environment specifications. results/feature_dictionary.csv (2,928 bytes) — Full data dictionary defining all 37 attributes, physical units, and provenance. results/label_circularity_audit.json (17,530 bytes) — Machine-readable variance decomposition and baseline comparison exports. results/genai_audit_bank.json (35,882 bytes) — 100 structured synthetic scenarios for LLM compliance auditing. results/genai_audit_review_sheet.csv (47,295 bytes) — Manual verification rubric with inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.85). It does not establish mine-site functional safety, nor does it claim active-mine physical twin synchronisation or autonomous braking actuation.

items.summary: Dataset description This dataset provides gap-filled daily, high-resolution binary snow cover maps for 12 eddy-covariance stations within the FLUXNET, ICOS, and i-Box networks distributed across the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps. The maps were generated to characterize surface snow conditions within the source areas of eddy-covariance measurements for the updated analysis of Scheidt et al. (2026). The dataset was specifically used to determine whether the area enclosed by a station’s 80% flux-footprint contour was snow covered and to calculate the snow-cover fraction (SCF) within that footprint. Footprint-scale SCF can be calculated from the maps as the proportion of valid pixels within the footprint classified as snow covered. The data cover the following eddy-covariance sites for the hydrological years (1 st October - 30 th September) from 2013/14 to 2023/24: Alp Weissenstein (CH-Aws), Switzerland Col du Lautaret (FR-CLt), France Früebüel (CH-Fru), Switzerland Monte Bondone (IT-MBo), Italy Mazia Pasture (IT-MtP), Italy Neustift (AT-Neu), Austria Nivolet (IT-NiG), Italy Torgnon (IT-Tor), Italy The i-Box observational network in the Inn Valley, Austria, comprising the Eggen (CS-SF1), Kolsass (CS-VF0), Hochhäuser (CS-NF27), and Weerberg (CS-NF10) stations For each station outside the i-Box network, the NetCDF files cover a 15 km × 15 km square centered on the station. Because the four i-Box stations are located close to one another, they are represented by a common 20 km × 20 km domain centered on the station cluster. The maps have a spatial resolution of 50 m and are provided in the WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N coordinate reference system (EPSG:32632). Files are organized by site and hydrological year. The binary snow cover condition variable represents daily snow-cover conditions, while the reconstruction_method variable distinguishes pixels obtained from high-resolution satellite observations from pixels reconstructed by the gap-filling procedure. High-resolution snow cover fraction maps were derived from Sentinel-2 MSI and Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 OLI imagery using SnowFLAKES ( Snow extent from applying a Flexible Learning Algorithm using KErnel-based Spectral unmixing ) at a resolution of 50m. SnowFLAKES is an unsupervised, image-adaptive snow-mapping approach developed for mountainous terrain and challenging observation conditions, including topographic shadows and variable illumination. The processing follows the approach described by Barella et al. (2022). Daily, spatially complete maps were generated by combining the available high-resolution snow observations with daily, lower-resolution MODIS SCF from the MOD10A1 product (Hall and Riggs, 2021). Gap filling and spatial downscaling were performed using an implementation adapted from the hierarchical multiresolution data-fusion method proposed by Premier et al. (2021). The approach uses spatial patterns learned from available optical observations to reconstruct snow-cover conditions on days without usable high-resolution satellite imagery. The resulting product represents daily binary snow presence at high spatial resolution. Raw Sentinel-2, Landsat, and MODIS imagery, eddy-covariance measurements, and flux footprint polygons are not included in this archive. The archive also includes an interactive Python viewer for the daily *_SC_GAM.nc snow-cover products. It can display snow-cover classes and reconstruction provenance over time, with station locations shown for context. Setup instructions and examples are provided in the README. items.summary: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.
items.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction

items.summary: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|μ|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|ρ|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.
items.title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer

items.summary: Scaling depth is a key route to stronger large language models, but Pre-LN architectures often suffer from depth-wise information dilution, limiting the effective use of deep layers. While cross-layer connectivity has proven effective at mitigating this problem, existing designs usually introduce additional computation or memory access. We revisit cross-layer KV sharing as an efficient form of such connectivity. Beyond cache compression, each KV reuse edge creates a direct gradient path from deep layers to source KV projections, turning KV sharing into an implicit structural regularizer for KV representation geometry. We provide a systematic analysis of this mechanism, showing that proper sharing topologies sharpen key retrieval directions while enriching the value content subspace, whereas existing adjacent or global-anchor designs do not fully exploit this effect. Motivated by this, we propose DepthGraft, a hierarchical KV-sharing architecture that reconstructs deep-layer KV from stride-aligned shallow-middle source pairs. DepthGraft distributes non-local gradient flow across source layers, while preserving prefill early completion and reducing KV cache by roughly one third. Experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters show consistent downstream improvements under both GQA and MLA. Notably, on the 16B MoE model, DepthGraft achieves a 7.0% absolute improvement on MMLU-Pro, along with gains of 6.6% on CMMLU and 6.4% on C3. These results validate the potential of DepthGraft as a scalable design for large-scale pretraining. The project page is available at https://github.com/jianke0604/DepthGraft.

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. items.summary: Reliable forensic evidence extraction from mobile SQLite databases is challenging because application schemas are undocumented, evolve across releases, and differ across operating systems, making schema-specific methods brittle and difficult to maintain. We present SNEEF, a symbolic-neural framework for context-aware evidence extraction that encodes each SQLite row as context-value pairs with standardized provenance metadata and column labels, uses a language model to recognize nine forensic entity types, and binds each accepted entity to its source table and row through the PA-EEP provenance protocol. We evaluate SNEEF against examiner-verified ground truth from five corpora built from public Android and iOS device images, spanning multiple application versions. SNEEF achieves an F1 score of 0.967 for evidence entities extracted from SQLite row content, excluding application names, compared with 0.728 for a context-free configuration, with consistent gains across all corpora. We also introduce an Evidence Failure Mode taxonomy to characterize why extraction errors occur.
items.title: A Symbolic-Neural Framework for Context-Aware Evidence Extraction from Mobile SQLite Databases

items.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. In one sentence: the matrix geometric mean can jump at singular matrices, every possible jump is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism refutes a published claim that the symbol of the geometric mean of two GLT matrix-sequences is always the geometric mean of their symbols. The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance matrices and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It need not be continuous at singular pairs. Theorem 1 shows that X is a limit of A j #B j with positive definite A j → A, B j → B exactly when X ≽ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N (a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones; the explicit elimination is the contribution). At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences, uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols can have geometric means with the wrong symbol (4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval) or no eigenvalue distribution at all. This refutes Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their article in Linear Algebra Appl. (2025); the failing step of the proof is located. Positive results: closure for every Kubo-Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; a one-sided theorem that the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope; and, for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, a sharp dichotomy (the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports). The classical two-dimensional discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ≼ A#B are earlier work and are credited. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and Markdown source), two figures with the script that draws them, an exact verifier (verify_exact.py, Python standard library only, 1,030 rational and Gaussian-rational checks of closed forms and finite assemblies, with a mutation self-test) and its retained output, the bibliography with its Crossref/arXiv records, the dated novelty ledger, a revision note, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs; the verifier checks finite exact identities, not the theorems' limits or quantifiers; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification). items.summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
items.title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

items.summary: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
items.title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

items.summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.
items.title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. items.summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. In the original penetration metric, perpetual-inventory robot capital preserves the estimates at 5 percent depreciation, but faster assumed depreciation counts the automotive installations behind the first stage as replacement rather than net additions, eliminating shock-level relevance at 10 percent and all relevance at 15 percent. The benchmark is reproducible and robust in sign, but it is identified from an automotive margin in historically industrial labor markets; that margin defines its scope and the concrete content of its exclusion restriction. More generally, coefficient robustness and breadth of identifying support are distinct properties that shift-share studies should report separately. items.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
items.title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel

items.summary: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
items.title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. items.summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
items.title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

items.summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
items.title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

items.summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. items.summary: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.
items.title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction

items.summary: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.
items.title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?

items.summary: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.
items.title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration

items.summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.
items.title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation

items.summary: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.
items.title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions

items.summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
items.title: Online Label-Free Gradient Matching for Continual Language Model Training

items.summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
items.title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

items.summary: Long-horizon tasks require large language model (LLM) agents to coordinate interdependent actions, a capability central to automating complex workflows. Stepwise group-based reinforcement learning provides finer credit than trajectory-level supervision, but reliable comparisons must account for differences in interaction history. Enforcing this consistency within the limited rollouts of each task can leave insufficient support for estimating action preferences. We propose Beyond-Local Policy Optimization (BLPO), which estimates task-progress advantages from experience shared across tasks and training updates. We summarize trajectory prefixes into task-progress states and abstract actions by their function, allowing corresponding decisions from different tasks to contribute to shared estimates. To control bias and noise from heterogeneous tasks, we accumulate context-relative returns in a global memory with balanced aggregation and reliability weighting. These global advantages complement local comparisons over normalized actions and trajectory-level credit without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B policies show improved task success over the evaluated baselines under matched training budgets. Further analyses show faster learning and shorter trajectories with little computational overhead.
items.title: BLPO: Beyond-Local Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents

items.summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
items.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
